```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4
)
```

`spei()`, `spi()` and the PET functions process many series at once. The
data can be:

- a **matrix**, with one series per column, for several stations;
- a **3-d array** with dimensions time × longitude × latitude, for gridded
  data.

Each series is fitted separately, with the same options, so the result is
the same as computing each series in a loop, but simpler.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(SPEI)
```

## Several stations: matrices

The `balance` dataset holds the monthly climatic water balance at 11
stations around the world, from January 1900. It is a data frame; we
convert it to a monthly time series matrix:

```{r}
data(balance)
bal <- ts(as.matrix(balance), start = c(1900, 1), frequency = 12)
dim(bal)
colnames(bal)
```

A single call computes the SPEI for all the stations:

```{r}
spei12 <- spei(bal, 12, verbose = FALSE)
class(spei12$fitted)
```

The result is a time series matrix with the same columns. The plot method
shows one panel per station, for up to ten stations; here, the first four:

```{r, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "SPEI-12 at Indore, Kimberley, Albuquerque and Valencia, one panel per station"}
plot(spei(bal[, 1:4], 12, verbose = FALSE))
```

The coefficients array has one set of parameters per station and calendar
month (parameter × station × month):

```{r}
dim(spei12$coefficients)
```

The reference period and the other options of `vignette("options")` work in
the same way. With `na.rm = TRUE`, each station can have its own gaps.

### PET for several stations

The PET functions also take matrices, with one latitude per column:

```{r}
data(wichita)
tmed <- ts(cbind(site1 = wichita$TMED, site2 = wichita$TMED + 2),
  start = c(1980, 1), frequency = 12
)
pet <- thornthwaite(tmed, lat = c(37.6, 40.1), verbose = FALSE)
head(pet)
```

## Gridded data: 3-d arrays

The `cruts4` dataset is a small grid of 2 × 3 cells in the central Pyrenees (Spain and France),
with the monthly water balance from CRU TS 4.05 for 1900–2019. Its
dimensions are time × longitude × latitude:

```{r}
data(cruts4)
dim(cruts4)
```

Arrays are processed in the same way, and the result has the same
dimensions:

```{r}
spei12_grid <- spei(cruts4, 12, verbose = FALSE)
dim(spei12_grid$fitted)
```

For example, the SPEI-12 of the last month (December 2019) in each cell:

```{r}
round(spei12_grid$fitted[1440, , ], 2)
```

An array can't be a time series, so without more information it is taken
to start in January, and a reference period would have to be given as
years counted from the first one. The arguments `start` and `frequency`
give the time information, as in `ts()`. With them the reference period
is given in calendar dates, here 1961–1990:

```{r}
spei12_ref <- spei(cruts4, 12,
  start = c(1900, 1),
  ref.start = c(1961, 1), ref.end = c(1990, 12), verbose = FALSE
)
```

The time dimension of the result is labelled with the months, so it can be
indexed by date. December 2019 again, now with the 1961–1990 reference
period:

```{r}
head(dimnames(spei12_ref$fitted)[[1]])
round(spei12_ref$fitted["2019-12", , ], 2)
```

Monthly labels are "YYYY-MM"; with other frequencies the periods are
numbered, e.g. "1961-P01" to "1961-P48" with `frequency = 48` (weekly
data, see `vignette("weekly")`). If the time `dimnames` of an array are
already monthly dates ("YYYY-MM" or "YYYY-MM-DD", as when they are read from
a NetCDF file), `start` is not needed: the time information is taken from
them.

The PET functions take arrays too, with latitude given as a longitude ×
latitude matrix:

```{r}
tmed <- array(rep(wichita$TMED, 6), dim = c(382, 2, 3))
lat <- matrix(c(42.25, 42.75, 43.25), nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
pet <- thornthwaite(tmed, lat, start = c(1980, 1), verbose = FALSE)
dim(pet)
```

The PET functions also take `start` (the first month; the frequency is
always 12), which sets the calendar month of each time step and labels the
time dimension of the result.

### Cells with no data

Grids often include cells with no data, such as the ocean in land datasets.
Those cells need `na.rm = TRUE`, and their index is `NA`:

```{r}
x <- cruts4
x[, 1, 1] <- NA
s <- spei(x, 12, na.rm = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
round(s$fitted[1440, , ], 2)
```

## Reading and writing NetCDF files

Gridded climate data are usually distributed as NetCDF files. The code below
sketches how to compute the SPEI from the CRU TS precipitation and PET files
with the `ncdf4` package. It is not run here, because it needs the files,
which are large.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(ncdf4)

pre_nc <- nc_open("cru_ts4.10.1901.2025.pre.dat.nc")
pet_nc <- nc_open("cru_ts4.10.1901.2025.pet.dat.nc")

# Variables are stored as longitude x latitude x time
pre <- ncvar_get(pre_nc, "pre") # mm per month
pet <- ncvar_get(pet_nc, "pet") # mm per day

# Convert PET to mm per month: multiply each time step by its number of
# days. `sweep()` applies the vector along the third (time) dimension;
# `pet * ndays` would recycle it along longitude instead.
dates <- as.Date(ncvar_get(pre_nc, "time"), origin = "1900-01-01")
ndays <- lubridate::days_in_month(dates)
pet <- sweep(pet, 3, ndays, "*")

# Put time first, as spei() expects
bal <- aperm(pre - pet, c(3, 1, 2))

spei12 <- spei(bal, 12, na.rm = TRUE, start = c(1901, 1), verbose = FALSE)

# Back to longitude x latitude x time for writing
out <- aperm(spei12$fitted, c(2, 3, 1))
```

The result can then be written with `ncdf4::ncvar_def()`,
`ncdf4::nc_create()` and `ncdf4::ncvar_put()`, using the dimensions of the
input file.

Note the conversion of PET to monthly values. When a vector is multiplied
by an array, R recycles the vector along the first dimension of the array,
not along time. The SPEIbase dataset was affected by this error until
version 2.13.0.

### Large grids

A global grid at 0.5° has about 67,000 land cells, and more than 1,500
months of data. Such arrays can exceed the memory of a desktop computer.
Two common ways to handle them:

- **Process the grid in blocks**, for example by bands of latitude, reading
  each block from the file with the `start` and `count` arguments of
  `ncvar_get()`, and writing each result before reading the next block.
- **Process the blocks in parallel**, for example with the `parallel` or
  `future.apply` packages. Each cell is fitted independently, so the result
  doesn't depend on how the grid is split.

### A complete example: SPEIbase

[SPEIbase](https://github.com/sbegueria/SPEIbase) is the code that produces
the global SPEI dataset distributed at <https://spei.csic.es>. It does
everything described in this section for the whole globe: it reads the CRU
TS precipitation and PET NetCDF files in bands of latitude, converts PET to
monthly values, computes the SPEI at time scales from 1 to 48 months in
parallel, and writes the results to NetCDF files. Its code is a good
starting point for processing other large gridded datasets.
